name: Erik Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work underground, not up poles, which surprises people. I'm a trainee on a city cable crew, so my day is a hole in the pavement on some busy street, a tent over it, and me as the jointer's mate: pumping out water, cutting back the old lead sheath, handing Hamid the right tool before he asks for it. We start at seven from the yard on Canal Street and we're usually in the hole by eight. I like the quiet down there, oddly, with the traffic going over your head. What wears me out is the kneeling and the paperwork, the permits and the photos for every joint.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up as a trainee at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Robots, funnily enough. I drove a forklift at a big distribution warehouse for twenty-six years, and in 2024 they brought in the automatic pickers and cut the night shift from forty of us to six. I was fifty-six, I had about three weeks of wages in the bank, and a mate from the union told me the electricity company was short of cable hands. So I'm the slowest learner on the crew, but I've already been replaced by a machine once, so I've got a head start on this conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that fuss and the holes still need digging. At the yard I'd probably wind up the young ones who keep saying their jobs are doomed. Online I'd share something from the union about how the money should've gone into wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I picked this job because I thought cables in the ground were safe from robots, after what happened at the warehouse. If AI turns out to be mostly hype, then I made the right call for once, and I can just get on with learning the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my training and try to pass my jointing module by next summer, which bumps my pay a bit. I'd use the AI app now and then, like I do, to explain a cable diagram in plain words before I ask Hamid something daft. And I'd try to get one month of money put by, which I've never managed since the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, a bit smug. Like I'd backed the right horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI app at work. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to stop myself looking stupid. If Hamid says something about three-core cable or a transition joint and I don't follow, I type it in at lunch and it explains it like I'm twelve. I always check with him after, though, because I'm not trusting a phone with eleven thousand volts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does getting one month put by look like, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I worked it out: about forty a week from my overtime into a separate account that I don't have a card for. It's been sitting at about two weeks' worth since spring because something always comes up. Last time it was the car's clutch, before that her mother's funeral.

S0.say: All that fuss, and the holes still need digging. He would tease the young ones who think their jobs are doomed and share a union post about money going to wages instead.
S0.think: He would be glad, because he chose cable work believing it was safe from robots after losing his warehouse job. If AI is mostly hype, he made the right call for once.
S0.do: Keeps training and aims to pass his jointing module by next summer for a small pay rise. Keeps using an AI app now and then to understand diagrams, and tries to save forty a week toward one month of savings.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like he backed the right horse.
S0.quote: I always check with him after, though, because I'm not trusting a phone with eleven thousand volts.
S0.fieldNote: Erik has already lost a job to robots, and he chose line work on purpose as a safer place. He uses AI quietly as a study aid but treats it with healthy suspicion. His savings plan is real but keeps getting knocked back by ordinary emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've seen this film before, and the workers need a say in how it's done this time. At the yard I'd tell people to join the union now, not after the letters go out. Online I'd post about what happened at the warehouse, because nobody believed me then either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think, here we go again, but slower. The paperwork side of my job would probably go to the machines first, the photos and permits, and I wouldn't miss it. What I'd worry about is if they decide one experienced jointer plus a robot arm can do what a jointer and a mate do now, because I'm the mate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to put me on whatever new kit they bring in, so I'm the one trained on it, not the one replaced by it. I'd get more active in the union branch, maybe stand as a workplace rep, which I said I'd never do. I'd keep up the savings and learn the AI tools they actually give us, once I've seen them work for someone else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not knocked over, but I'd be watching the noticeboard every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never stand as a rep. What's changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the warehouse, the rep was a lad of twenty-eight who'd never seen a redundancy, and he got flattened in the meetings. I've been through it. If there's going to be a slow squeeze, someone who knows how it goes should be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not like 2024, it's slower, we'll see it coming. She works in a care home, and she'd probably say her job's safer than mine, and she'd be right. Then she'd ask whether we can still go to her sister's in the spring, and I'd say yes, but we'd go by coach.

S1.say: We've seen this film before, and workers need a say this time. He would urge colleagues to join the union now and share his warehouse story online.
S1.think: He expects the paperwork to go first, which he wouldn't miss. His real fear is that one experienced jointer plus a robot arm replaces the jointer-and-mate pair, because he is the mate.
S1.do: Asks to be trained on any new kit the company brings in and steps up as a union workplace rep. Keeps saving and learns the AI tools once he has seen them work for others.
S1.feel: Uneasy, checking the noticeboard every morning without being knocked over.
S1.quote: I'd tell her it's not like 2024, it's slower, we'll see it coming.
S1.fieldNote: Erik's past displacement makes him both wary and practical: he wants to be the person trained on the new kit. The decision to stand as a union rep is a real shift, driven by watching an inexperienced rep fail at the warehouse. He stays cautious about tools until others have proven them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happened at the warehouse, only to everyone at once, and the government has to step in. At work I'd be telling people the union needs to demand the company keep crews on through the change. Online I'd be angry, I won't lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, with a tiny pension because I lost half of it cashing out after the warehouse. If robots can do cable joints by 2028, I've been replaced by machines twice in four years. I don't think there's a third job out there for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Lena and cut everything we can: the car goes, she gets the bus, no holidays. I'd go to the union and push for a deal where older workers keep their jobs till pension age while the robots come in. I'd find out what government support there is, properly, because I'm not too proud after last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being punched in the same bruise. I'd be up at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd been replaced twice. What does that do to how you see yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me feel like I keep choosing the wrong door. I'm not stupid; I learned the forklift, I'm learning the cables. But there's only so many times you can start again at the bottom before you just feel like the bottom is where you live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill that goes unpaid if it comes to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, then the phone contracts. The rent we'd protect at all costs, because we're renting from the housing association and losing that place would be the end of us. Lena's said she'd pick up extra shifts, but she's sixty too and her back's no better than mine.

S2.say: This is the warehouse story happening to everyone at once, and the government has to step in. He would push the union to demand crews are kept on through the change.
S2.think: He would be sixty with a tiny pension, having cashed out half of it after the warehouse. Being replaced by machines twice in four years would leave him with no realistic third job.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard in the first week, selling the car and dropping holidays. Pushes the union for older workers to keep jobs until pension age and seeks out government support without shame.
S2.feel: Like being punched in the same bruise, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: There's only so many times you can start again at the bottom before you just feel like the bottom is where you live.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's fear here is shaped by having already been through a robot redundancy. He moves quickly and practically, but the language turns raw when he talks about starting over again. He openly accepts government support, which fits both his politics and his experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it properly, so let's see them do it properly. At the branch I'd want a written plan: who gets retrained, who gets bridged to pension, and when. I'd post about it, but more calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, which isn't retirement but it's close enough to bargain over. I'd think, if I can finish my jointing ticket and be useful during the changeover, I might get to see it out. It's still a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my jointing qualification in the first eighteen months, no matter what, because a qualified jointer is worth more in any deal. I'd lobby through the union for an early-pension bridge for over-sixties. And I'd try to get that savings pot up to two months, maybe by selling the second-hand bike and some of my old tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got a list, and lists help me. It's the not knowing that's worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said lists help. What's at the top of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jointing ticket, union bridge deal, savings, in that order. Then something soft, like teaching my grandson how to change a plug, because I like the idea of someone in the family still knowing how electricity actually works. Silly, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the yard, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Dev, who started the same month I did. He's twenty-two, renting, and he thinks he's set for life because he's in a trade. I'd want to tell him not to make the mistake I made of thinking any job is safe, but he wouldn't listen; I wouldn't have at his age.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do it properly, so let's see them do it properly. He would want a written union plan on retraining, pension bridges and timing.
S3.think: At sixty-three he would be close enough to retirement to bargain. If he finishes his jointing ticket and is useful during the changeover, he might see it out, though it's still a gamble.
S3.do: Finishes his jointing qualification within eighteen months and lobbies through the union for an early-pension bridge for over-sixties. Tries to raise savings to two months by selling a bike and old tools.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a list.
S3.quote: I like the idea of someone in the family still knowing how electricity actually works.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Erik's fear into a plan, with clear priorities and timing. His concern for younger colleague Dev shows the lesson he took from the warehouse. The small wish to teach his grandson about electricity was touching and unexpected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being thrown on the scrapheap. At work I'd tell the young ones to start planning now. To my mates I'd say this is the one where we've got no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years takes me past sixty-six, so for me it's mostly about holding on. I'd be a qualified jointer by then, probably training the robots or watching them. My worry would be my sons, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, finish my training, and save a bit more each year. I'd push the union for proper training money for the young ones, since they're the ones with thirty years left. I'd talk to my lad who drives a delivery van about what he's doing next, because his job's gone in that picture for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the boys. For me it feels almost like a reprieve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your son who drives a delivery van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't wait for the letter like I did. Look now, while you've got a wage coming in. He's got a mortgage and a baby on the way, and I'd rather he was annoyed with me now than in my shoes at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels like a reprieve. Do you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. I said the warehouse was safe too, and look what happened. But ten years is a long time; I've been at this for two and I already feel like I've lived three lives.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being thrown on the scrapheap. He would tell younger workers to start planning now.
S4.think: With ten years he will be past sixty-six, so for him it is mostly about holding on. His real worry is his sons, not himself.
S4.do: Keeps working, finishes his training and saves a bit more each year. Pushes the union for training money for young workers and urges his delivery-driver son to look for new work now.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his sons, but close to a reprieve for himself.
S4.quote: I'd rather he was annoyed with me now than in my shoes at fifty-six.
S4.fieldNote: A decade shifts Erik's attention from himself to his sons. He doesn't fully trust the sense of safety, because he trusted the warehouse too. His advice to his son is shaped entirely by his own regret about waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I've already lived a small version of it, and I know I can't do it twice. What would help is a deal that keeps older workers on till pension age while the machines come in, and some real money for retraining young people. Not an app, not a webinar, actual money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to have already been replaced once. It changes how you hear everything, every new machine, every meeting. I've got a forklift licence in a drawer that nobody will ever ask to see again.

headlineQuote: I've got a forklift licence in a drawer that nobody will ever ask to see again.
portrait: Erik Wagner is a 58-year-old trainee on a city underground cable crew, who joined after automatic pickers cut his warehouse night shift in 2024. He lives in a housing association flat with his partner Lena, a care home worker, and has about two weeks of savings and a small pension. He uses AI now and then to understand diagrams but always checks with his jointer. Through the milder pictures he plans to finish his jointing ticket and step up as a union rep, while the 2028 picture hits him as a second blow he can't absorb. With ten years, his worry moves to his sons.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because he has already been replaced by machines once and doesn't believe he could start over a second time.
whatWouldHelp: A deal that keeps older workers on until pension age while machines come in, plus real money, not apps or webinars, for retraining young people.
